notes.why: The main sense of a calling bat is an echo picture: brightness from echo strength, refreshed call by call, in a cone of 60 to 90 degrees. Needs a depth source (LiDAR or a depth model) and a new drawing mode. Hard. Until then the entry draws the coarse eyes with the call-rate hold.
Daubenton's bat has its sharp area in the upper retina, which looks at the lower field (the sheet's inference). The engine places sharpness only at the centre or along the horizon.
Big brown bats steer by the magnetic field (Holland 2006). Reading the sensor is easy; there is no basis yet for drawing it.

rows: A big brown bat calls 5 to 10 times a second while searching, 20 to 80 times while closing in, and up to about 170 times in the final buzz. Each call returns one snapshot, so the picture holds, then jumps, about seven times a second. That rendering is this app’s invention.
From the delay of each echo, a big brown bat judges distance to within about 1.5 centimetres with its short hunting calls, and only to 15 centimetres or worse with its long search calls.
A bat hears an insect’s echo from about 2 to 14 metres away, depending on the bat and the insect, and a forest edge from up to about 50 metres. Beyond that, its calls return nothing it can hear.
A big brown bat swings its beam of sound from one object to the next with an accuracy of about 5 degrees. The beam spreads over a cone of 60 to 90 degrees, about as wide as this camera’s view.
Daubenton’s bat, an insect-eating relative, resolves about 0.6 cycles per degree to your 60, a hundredth of yours. The screen is blurred to match.
In one test a big brown bat could no longer tell things apart by sight once the light fell to between 0 and 0.0008 lux. Shadows are lifted to suggest it.
Some bats have a cone for ultraviolet and some have lost it, and no phone records ultraviolet. In two leaf-nosed bats only 2 to 4 in a hundred light receptors are cones, so colour is drained here.
A calling bat hears the distance to everything its calls reach, and a phone’s microphone cannot hear those calls.
Big brown bats steer home by the Earth’s magnetic field, which the picture does not draw.

With &draw=clap and the microphone on, the picture stays dark until you clap or click, and then it shows for a moment. A phone cannot hear echoes the way a bat does, so the drawing stands in for them and is the app's.

sound.say: This view lights the picture when it hears a clap or a click, as a bat sees by its echoes. Tap to let it listen through the microphone. Nothing is recorded or kept.
